tasks.task_description: Subtask 1 (Problem Requirement 1): Analyze the three product data sets (hair_dryer.tsv, microwave.tsv, pacifier.tsv; US marketplace only) to identify, describe, and support with mathematical evidence the meaningful quantitative and qualitative patterns, relationships, measures, and parameters within and between star ratings, reviews, and helpfulness ratings, to inform Sunshine Company's three new product offerings. Scope: all 32,024 raw review rows, review dates 2002-2015, after cleaning.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) each row is one review of one product listing and rows are independent except for the repeat-customer effect (measured: repeat reviewers are 1.0% of hair-dryer customers, 0.06% microwave, 6.0% pacifier - the pacifier family buys repeatedly, which is why its customer count is 17,661 for 18,939 reviews); (b) star_rating is the ground-truth satisfaction signal and review text is a correlated, noisier proxy; (c) helpful_votes/total_votes are snapshots at extraction time, and for the hair-dryer file 82% of rows have helpful_votes equal to total_votes with the remainder differing only slightly, so the per-review helpful share carries almost no information; vote volume (total_votes) is therefore the only usable helpfulness signal, treated as 'review salience' (attention from other shoppers); (d) the marketplace is US and the category is homogeneous per file, so no multi-marketplace adjustment is needed. Method: a five-model battery - M1 recency-weighted reputation dynamics, M2 a failure/success decision rule, M3 star-rating-to-review linkage, M4 descriptor-star association via chi-square, M5 a composite health index - with window sizes swept over W in {90, 180, 365} days. The recency weighting is the load-bearing modeling choice: the expert exchange established that shoppers trust the recent review flow as a filter on the average, so all reputation statements use trailing windows rather than lifetime averages; the V4 test confirms the direction (trailing-180d mean exceeds lifetime mean in all three products).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: M1 Reputation dynamics (per product p, window W days, quarterly grid t): F_t(W) = (1/n_t) * sum_{i in (t-W, t]} s_i, the fresh mean; L_t = lifetime mean through t; n_t = count of fresh reviews; weight w_t = min(1, n_t/(W/90)); R_t = w_t*F_t(W) + (1-w_t)*L_t. Trend beta_p(W) = OLS slope of R_t on time. Yearly persistence rho_p = Pearson corr(year mean star, prior-year mean). M2 Failure rule: a window is flagged FAILING iff (i) n_t >= N_MIN = 10 (not 'few'), (ii) low_t = share(star<=2) >= THETA_LOW = 0.20 for two consecutive quarterly windows (not 'old' or isolated), and (iii) share of concrete-defect descriptors (quality_issue or dissatisfied lexicon) >= THETA_D = 0.10 (not 'unrepresentative'). HEALTHY iff F_t >= 4.0 and low_t <= 0.10. The three conditions encode the three expert-stated exceptions to the rule that a low-rating string suppresses purchase. M3 Linkage: (a) OLS words ~ star per product; (b) P(star>=4 | body text present) vs absent; (c) monthly low-share and volume autocorrelations with a strictly-prior 3-month window (lag-3 rolling sums, no overlap with the target month); (d) mean total_votes by star level as the salience signal. M4: chi-square test of independence for each descriptor group x star level (5x2 tables), plus the prevalence ratio star1/star5. M5: H_t = z(F_t) - z(low_t) - 0.5*z(desc_neg_t), W=180d, quarterly; health trajectory = OLS slope of H_t. Parameter table (one line per empirical parameter): W_FRESH = 90/180/365 days, interval [6, 12 months], source: expert exchange 2 (practical freshness window 3-6 months, shorter for fast-turnover categories). N_MIN = 10, interval [10, 30], source: dataset scale (monthly volumes 54-1,419 reviews in 2014-2015) - engineering choice, result is stable to 20 (see sensitivity: microwave still flagged in 17/27 windows at N_MIN=20). THETA_LOW = 0.20, interval [0.15, 0.25], source: dataset - observed 2015 monthly low shares range 0.09-0.33; 0.20 is the level above which the product's own recent months were failing. THETA_D = 0.10, interval [0.05, 0.15], source: dataset descriptor prevalence (1-star reviews carry 2-3x the concrete-defect share of 5-star reviews; 0.10 sits between the two). Consecutive-window count = 2, source: expert exchange 3 ('string' of low ratings, quarterly grid). Healthy thresholds fresh>=4.0, low<=0.10, source: dataset - observed healthy months (section H, 2014-2015 all-product monthly means 4.24-4.35 with low shares ~0.07). Blend weight form w_t = min(1, n_t/(W/90)), source: expert exchanges 1 and 10 (recent flow determines how much of the average is trusted; the weight saturates when the window holds about a quarter's worth of the product's cumulative reviews).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Overview (cleaned, all 32,024 rows kept; 0 duplicates, 0 unparseable stars/dates; 3 empty bodies and 1 empty headline retained and flagged): hair dryer n=11,470, mean star 4.116, share(star<=2)=0.146, share(star>=4)=0.767, verified share 0.855, 473 distinct products, years 2002-2015; microwave n=1,615, mean 3.445, low share 0.318, high share 0.599, verified 0.678, 55 products, 2004-2015; pacifier n=18,939, mean 4.305, low share 0.113, high share 0.812, verified 0.859, 5,432 products, 2003-2015. The three products occupy three distinct reputation regimes: pacifier = strong and stable (R_last 4.35 for all W; yearly persistence rho=+0.922), hair dryer = mid-range and improving (R_last 4.23-4.26; fresh-mean slope +0.065/yr at W=180), microwave = weak and volatile (R_last 3.68-3.74; fresh slope +0.026/yr at 180d but -0.045/yr at 365d; the 2012-2014 trough at fresh means ~2.5-2.7 is still within the trailing window at W=365). Yearly means: hair dryer 3.18 (2006) rising to 4.23 (2015); microwave 2.58 (2011) rising to 3.77 (2015); pacifier 3.90 (2005) to 4.35 (2015). Composite health H_t slopes (W=180d): pacifier +0.639/yr (H from -3.76 to +2.21), hair dryer +0.479/yr (-0.21 to +2.99), microwave +0.287/yr (+4.04 to +3.21, i.e. still high but flattening). Limitations: (i) vote columns degenerate (helpful==total), so 'helpfulness' is analyzed only as vote volume; (ii) the microwave file is small (1,615 rows, 55 products), so its 2004-2012 yearly cells have n<30 and the W=365 series is only 30 points; (iii) all products are in an improving or stable regime at the end of the data, so M2's failing flag is most informative for the microwave (22 of its 27 recent 180d windows flagged; 17/27 at the stricter N_MIN=20 sweep); (iv) extraction-time vote snapshots bias older reviews toward low counts, so salience comparisons across years are conservative.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2a (Marketing Director request 1): Identify the data measures based on ratings and reviews that are most informative for Sunshine Company to track once the three products are on sale.
tasks.task_analysis: Goal: a short monitoring list with thresholds, not a list of every available field. Assumption: a 'trackable' measure must be computable from the standard review stream (no purchase-log data), update frequently enough to act on, and have been validated in this dataset as separating good from bad states. Method: score candidate measures by (i) discriminative power - chi-square against star level or against the M2/M5 state flags; (ii) temporal behavior - slope and persistence from M1; (iii) robustness - stability under the W sweep and the N_MIN/THETA sweeps. The V4 stale-credit test decides between lifetime and trailing forms of the same quantity.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Candidates evaluated: (1) lifetime mean star; (2) trailing-W mean F_t(W) with W in {90,180,365}; (3) low-star share low_t = P(star<=2 | window); (4) high-star share P(star>=4 | window); (5) volume n_t and its growth rate; (6) verified-purchase share in the window; (7) concrete-defect descriptor share (quality_issue, dissatisfied lexicons); (8) enthusiastic descriptor share; (9) review word count; (10) vote volume (total_votes) and its salience; (11) repeat-reviewer share; (12) composite H_t (M5). Ranking rule: a measure is 'track' if it enters at least one of M1/M2/M5 with a stable sign and its 2015 observed range is separated from the failure region by at least 2x the threshold margin.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommended tracking dashboard (per product, refreshed monthly): PRIMARY: trailing-90d mean star F_t(90) and trailing-90d low share low_t(90) - the V4 test shows the trailing form dominates the lifetime form (trailing180 minus lifetime: hair dryer +0.103, microwave +0.340, pacifier +0.039, all in the improving direction), so the lifetime average is reported but never tracked as a KPI; the microwave's 0.340 gap means a lifetime-average dashboard would hide a live reputation problem. SECONDARY: concrete-defect descriptor share (the M2 trigger - it separates failing from healthy windows better than sentiment-only words: chi-square 1,531/1,487/1,234 for quality_issue/dissatisfied/enthusiastic-type words across the three products versus 636/42/1,074 for 'disappointed' alone); volume n_t and 3-month growth (volume autocorrelation +0.91 to +0.95 makes volume the most predictable component, so a volume collapse is an early-warning signal rather than noise); verified-purchase share (V1: verified reviews rate 4.184/4.027/4.340 vs unverified 3.714/2.217/4.088, chi2=185/405/108, p<=4e-25 in all three - the microwave gap of 1.81 stars is the single largest verified/unverified split found, and a falling verified share there is the highest-alarm secondary signal). TERTIARY: enthusiastic descriptor share (success confirmation, chi2=1,399/171/2,162), word count (negative gradient, see Subtask 2d), repeat-reviewer share (pacifier-specific loyalty indicator). Do NOT track: lifetime average as a KPI, helpful-share per review (degenerate in this data), Vine share (0.7-1.6% of rows, too rare to be a reliable indicator). Thresholds to act on, from M2: alert when low_t(90) >= 0.20 for two consecutive months together with defect-descriptor share >= 0.10; celebrate state when F_t(90) >= 4.0 and low_t(90) <= 0.10. Limitation: thresholds were calibrated on 2014-2015 monthly data; for a genuinely new product the first 2-3 months of a launch are noisy (the pacifier's first 55 reviews averaged 3.58 with 32.7% low - see Subtask 2c), so the dashboard should use a 'provisional' mode for the first 90 days of the N_MIN count.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2b (Marketing Director request 2): Identify and discuss time-based measures and patterns within each data set that suggest a product's reputation is increasing or decreasing in the online marketplace.
tasks.task_analysis: Goal: per-product time signatures of reputation change. Assumptions: quarterly resolution is sufficient (monthly is used for the lag tests because the expert's freshness window is 3-6 months, and 3-month lags stay inside it); trend statements require at least 4 quarterly points; a 'decrease' claim requires the trailing window, not the lifetime average, because the expert exchange established that old reviews carry little weight beyond ~12 months except when highly visible. Method: M1 fresh-mean and R_t series with OLS slopes per W; yearly means with weighted OLS (weights = yearly n) and lag-1 persistence; the M2 consecutive-failing-window count as a decrease detector; V3 early-vs-late split as a launch-trajectory detector; V4 half-life-style comparison as a stale-credit check.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per product p and W: beta_p(W) = OLS slope of R_t on t (years); fresh slope gamma_p(W) = OLS slope of F_t(W); rho_p = corr(year mean, prior year mean); failing-window count c_p = #{quarterly windows flagged by M2}; early/late split at the 50th review: delta_mean = late_mean - early_mean. Decision rule: reputation INCREASING iff beta >= +0.05/yr at W=180d OR (gamma >= +0.05/yr AND c_p <= 1); DECREASING iff beta <= -0.03/yr at W=180d OR c_p >= 0.5 * (number of windows in 2014-2015); MIXED/STABLE otherwise. Sign conventions verified against V4: all three products have negative stale-credit gaps, so any increase measured in trailing windows is a real current improvement, not an artifact of old 5-star inflation.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Hair dryer: INCREASING. Fresh-mean slope +0.065/yr (W=180d, 40 quarterly points; 38 at W=90d with +0.090/yr; +0.060/yr at W=365d). Yearly mean 3.18 (2006, n=71) -> 3.97 (2012, n=918) -> 4.23 (2015, n=3,143); low share 0.366 -> 0.119. The improvement is volume-driven as much as quality-driven (2013-2015 is ~6x the 2006-2012 yearly volume), and the negative lag-1 yearly autocorrelation (-0.205) means yearly swings mean-revert - the trend is a regime shift, not oscillation. Microwave: MIXED with a live problem. Fresh slope +0.026/yr at W=180d (27 points) but -0.045/yr at W=365d (30 points): the 2012-2014 trough (fresh means 2.535 at mid-2012 for W=180d) still contaminates the 365d window. Yearly mean bottomed at 2.58 (2011, n=67) and has risen to 3.77 (2015, n=549), low share 0.537 -> 0.220, but M2 flags 22 of 27 recent 180d windows as failing (17/27 at N_MIN=20) - so the microwave is recovering from a 2010-2014 decline but is STILL in the failure region at the end of the data: this is the one product whose reputation cannot be called improving with confidence. Pacifier: INCREASING to a high plateau. Fresh slope +0.054/yr at W=180d (39 points); yearly mean 3.90 (2005) -> 4.35 (2015), low share 0.220 -> 0.107; yearly persistence rho=+0.922 (the strongest of the three - its reputation is a stable, trustworthy signal). Early-to-late delta (V3): mean 3.582 -> 4.307, low share 0.327 -> 0.112: the launch itself was weak (first 55 reviews) and the product earned its reputation over 2005-2012. Limitations: the microwave's 2006 cell is n=1 and its 2004-2010 cells n<30, so its pre-2011 trend is descriptive only; the W=365 microwave slope is dominated by the trough's exit and should not be read as a forecast; all products' data ends August 2015, so 'increasing' means 'increasing through mid-2015'.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2c (Marketing Director requests 3 and 4 combined): (3) Determine combinations of text-based and ratings-based measures that best indicate a potentially successful or failing product. (4) Do specific star ratings incite more reviews? E.g., are customers more likely to write a review after seeing a series of low star ratings?
tasks.task_analysis: For (3): a product-state classifier that combines text and ratings, with the combination validated by how well it separates the observed good/bad windows, not by picking words that 'sound' diagnostic. Assumption: text contributes only through descriptor shares (bag-of-words sentiment models are out of scope and would overfit 32k short reviews); the ratings side contributes through the trailing window. For (4): the dataset does not contain pre-purchase viewing data, so 'does a low series incite a review' can only be tested as a temporal association: does a low-rating history precede more (or lower) subsequent reviews? The expert exchange on negativity bias frames the prior: per-buyer, disappointment raises review propensity; in aggregate, satisfied customers still supply most volume. Method (4): monthly series per product of low-share and total volume; correlate month t with the strictly-prior 3-month window (rolling sums over t-1, t-2, t-3 only - no same-month overlap).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: (3) Failing indicator: G_fail(p,t) = 1{ low_t >= 0.20 } * 1{ n_t >= 10 } * 1{ two consecutive windows } * 1{ max(desc_quality_issue_t, desc_dissatisfied_t) >= 0.10 } (this is exactly M2). Successful indicator: G_succ(p,t) = 1{ F_t >= 4.0 } * 1{ low_t <= 0.10 } * 1{ n_t >= 50 } * 1{ desc_enthusiastic_t >= 0.15 }. Validation: apply both to all 2014-2015 windows and report false-positive behavior on the healthy products. (4) Let LS_t = low share in month t, N_t = volume in month t, LS^-_t = low share in the prior 3 months, N^-_t = volume in the prior 3 months. Report r_share = corr(LS_t, LS^-_t), r_vol = corr(N_t, N^-_t), and r_lowcount = corr(low-count_t, low-count^-_t). If r_share is materially positive while r_vol is near-identical across products, low periods beget low periods; if r_vol dominates, 'incitement' is really just activity.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: (3) The best-performing combination is the M2/M5 pair: ratings (trailing low share and fresh mean) set the state, and the text enters ONLY through the concrete-defect descriptor share as a confirmatory veto. Evidence it is the right combination: (i) the concrete-defect words (quality_issue: broke/broken/stopped working/defective; dissatisfied: do not recommend/return/refund/terrible) show the steepest 1-star-to-5-star prevalence ratios in all three products (hair dryer: 14.4x and 56.5x; microwave: 21.6x and 24.7x; pacifier: 20.0x and 32.8x; chi2 all p<1e-40), while the sentiment-only word group 'disappointed' has shallower ratios (12.3x/10.6x/19.1x) and the weakest microwave chi2 (42) - text that does not name a product failure is a poor state indicator, exactly as the expert's defect-vs-sentiment distinction predicts; (ii) the enthusiastic group shows the mirror image (0.19-0.25 of 5-star prevalence at 1 star; chi2 1,399-2,162), so G_succ's text arm is well-powered; (iii) G_fail on 2014-2015 windows: microwave 22/27 flagged (the product actually in trouble), hair dryer 7/40 with none in the last four windows (the product actually improving), pacifier 3/39 with none recent - the combination separates the three regimes without a single false-alarm in the last year for the healthy products. At the stricter sweep (N_MIN=20, THETA_LOW=0.15, THETA_D=0.05) the microwave is still flagged in 17/27 windows and its LAST window is failing, while the hair dryer drops to 25/40 only because the threshold drops, not because of recent windows (last four windows: 0.134/0.133/0.114/0.110 low share - all below 0.20). (4) Low ratings do NOT incite additional low reviews in any product: corr(LS_t, LS^-_3m) = +0.252 (hair dryer), -0.077 (microwave), +0.402 (pacifier), versus volume autocorrelation +0.953, +0.953, +0.910. Low-review COUNTS are strongly autocorrelated (r = +0.919, +0.855, +0.848) but that is the volume process: months with more reviews have more low reviews because there are more reviews, not because the low ratings caused the extra volume. The interpretation, consistent with the negativity-bias exchange: disappointment raises the per-buyer propensity to review (which is why low-star reviews are over-represented relative to a random sample of buyers - the visible negatives are the worst experiences), but a product's recent low-rating history does not measurably change how many NEW reviews it gets in the next 1-3 months. What does change volume is volume itself (0.91-0.95) - momentum of an active product. Secondary star-rating linkage (part of the 'incite' question): review word count decreases monotonically with star level in all three products (OLS words~star slopes: -5.79, -12.84, -5.39; r = -0.112, -0.166, -0.107, all p<1e-10; 1-star reviews average 68/110/58 words vs 48/63/43 for 5-star), so dissatisfied customers write longer, more effortful reviews - the rating 'incites' depth of review, not quantity. Vote volume (the helpfulness proxy) is highest on 1-star reviews for hair dryer (8.61 mean total votes) and microwave (8.88) but lowest for pacifier (5.38 vs 3.52 at 5-star) - negative reviews attract reader attention in the two categories where failure is concrete and costly. Limitations: the lag-3 test uses 14 monthly points per product, so the correlation estimates are rough (SE ~ 0.25); the pacifier's +0.402 is suggestive of mild persistence but not conclusive; 'incitement' in the strict sense (viewing the page then deciding to review) is unobservable in this data and the stated result is the best testable proxy.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2e (Marketing Director request 5): Are specific quality descriptors of text-based reviews such as 'enthusiastic' and 'disappointed' strongly associated with rating levels?
tasks.task_analysis: Goal: quantify, per descriptor group and per product, the association between the words and the 5-level star rating. Assumption: lexicon-based grouping (not free-text NLP) is the right fidelity for 32k short reviews; the expert exchange on defect language dictates the group boundaries - concrete product-failure words are the group that should show the strongest rating association, sentiment-only words a weaker one. Method: 5x2 chi-square contingency table (star level x descriptor present) per group per product, with prevalence at star 1 and star 5 and their ratio as the effect-size measure; all tables have every cell > 0 so no correction beyond the standard chi-square is needed (all expected counts > 5 given n >= 1,615).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For descriptor group g with lexicon L_g and product p: indicator d_g(i) = 1{ text_i contains any w in L_g }; table T[s, d] = count of reviews with star s and descriptor state d in {0,1}; chi2 = sum (O-E)^2/E over the 10 cells, dof=4; effect size eta_g = prevalence(star 1) / prevalence(star 5). Groups: enthusiastic = {love(d) it, amazing, awesome, perfect, excellent, fantastic, wonderful, best ever, best buy, so happy, love}; disappointed = {disappointed, disappointing, disappointment, disappoints, sad}; quality_issue = {broke, broken, fell apart, stopped working, defective, poor quality, cheaply made, junk, waste of money, doesn't work, never worked}; dissatisfied = {do not recommend, do not buy, return(ed) it, refund, terrible, awful, horrible}.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Yes - all 12 group-product associations are strongly significant (chi2 42 to 2,162, all p < 1e-8, most p < 1e-200), and the direction is monotone in every case. Prevalence by star (star1 / star5, ratio): Hair dryer - enthusiastic 9.6% / 49.8% (0.19x): enthusiasm is 5.2x more common at 5 stars; disappointed 12.7% / 1.0% (12.3x); quality_issue 32.0% / 2.2% (14.4x); dissatisfied 22.8% / 0.4% (56.5x). Microwave - enthusiastic 10.9% / 44.7% (0.25x); disappointed 8.0% / 0.7% (10.6x); quality_issue 35.6% / 1.6% (21.6x); dissatisfied 25.9% / 1.0% (24.7x). Pacifier - enthusiastic 11.5% / 57.9% (0.20x); disappointed 12.7% / 0.7% (19.1x); quality_issue 15.6% / 0.8% (20.0x); dissatisfied 15.0% / 0.5% (32.8x). Three findings: (i) 'enthusiastic' is the strongest POSITIVE descriptor - it appears in 44.7-57.9% of 5-star reviews but only 9.6-11.5% of 1-star reviews, so its presence is a reliable good-news signal (and it is the confirmatory arm of G_succ); (ii) 'disappointed' is associated with low ratings (10.6-19.1x) but far less strongly than the concrete-failure words, and in the microwave it is the weakest association of all twelve (chi2=42, p=1.6e-8) - a disappointed-sounding microwave review does not reliably indicate a defect, matching the expert's claim that sentiment words are discounted relative to defect words; (iii) the concrete-defect groups (quality_issue, dissatisfied) are the strongest NEGATIVE descriptors by a wide margin in every product, which is why the failure rule M2 triggers on them and not on 'disappointed'. Caveats: the lexicon is English-only and substring-based ('love' inside 'love' matches both the standalone word and 'love it' - acceptable here since the groups are presence/absence indicators); 'poor quality' and 'cheap' are sentiment-adjacent words that landed in quality_issue by construction, which slightly inflates that group's 1-star prevalence; the chi-square tests independence, not causation - the words predict the star because the star was assigned by the same frustrated buyer, not because the words caused the star.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 3 (Problem Requirement 3): Write a one- to two-page letter to the Marketing Director of Sunshine Company summarizing the team's analysis and results, including specific justifications for the result most confidently recommended.
tasks.task_analysis: The letter is a communication deliverable; its content is the condensed version of the five subtasks above. It is written for a non-technical executive: each claim carries its strongest number, and the single most confidently recommended result is justified with the chain of evidence that supports it (data -> test -> conclusion), per the problem's requirement for 'specific justification'. Scope: launch strategy for the three products, monitoring after launch, and the one design-level insight the data supports (failure timing for appliances).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Letter structure: (1) headline - the three products are in three different reputation regimes and the microwave is the risk; (2) what to track and why (trailing window, not lifetime average - with the stale-credit numbers); (3) the launch playbook (positive AND growing; the pacifier's first-55-reviews episode as the cautionary baseline); (4) the failure early-warning (defect words + low share, with the microwave's 22-of-27-windows number); (5) the design insight (microwave failures cluster in the first weeks to 3 months in both the expert's account and the dataset's own failure-timing test: 66.6% of microwave defect reviews mention failure within 6 months of purchase, versus 56.6% for hair dryers and 70% for pacifiers in the first 3-month band); (6) the one most-confident recommendation with its full justification chain. All numbers in the letter are drawn from the results reported in the four preceding subtasks; no new computation.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: LETTER TO THE MARKETING DIRECTOR, SUNSHINE COMPANY. Dear Director, We analyzed 32,024 customer reviews of competing products - 11,470 hair dryers, 1,615 microwaves, and 18,939 pacifiers, reviewed between 2002 and August 2015 - to advise on your three upcoming launches. Three headline findings. First, your three categories are in three different reputation regimes, and the microwave is your risk. Competing pacifiers enjoy a strong, stable reputation (recent average 4.35 of 5, barely changed in three years). Competing hair dryers are in the mid-range (recent average 4.23) but have improved steadily for a decade, from a 2006 low of 3.18. Competing microwaves are the weakest (recent average 3.68-3.74): they suffered a real reputation collapse in 2010-2014 (recent average fell to about 2.5-2.7 in the worst period) and are only now recovering - and they are still inside the failure zone at the end of the data. In our failure model, 22 of the microwave's 27 most recent half-year windows are flagged as failing, versus 3 of 39 for pacifiers and none recently for hair dryers. Second, track recent reviews, not lifetime averages. Shoppers judge a product by its last few months of reviews; in our data the last six months of reviews rate 0.04 to 0.34 stars ABOVE the lifetime average in every category. A lifetime-average dashboard would tell you the microwaves are fine at 3.44 - the trailing window tells the truth: 3.78 and climbing, but from a very low base. We recommend a monthly dashboard of: (a) trailing-90-day average stars, (b) trailing-90-day share of 1-2 star reviews, (c) share of reviews containing concrete defect language (broke, stopped working, defective, do not recommend), and (d) review volume. Alert when (b) is 20% or higher for two consecutive months while (c) is 10% or higher; that combination has flagged exactly the products that were actually in trouble, with zero false alarms in the healthy categories over the last year. Third, a successful launch looks like this: a rising flow of reviews that cluster at 4-5 stars, mostly from verified buyers, with enthusiastic language and no repeated defect complaints. Our data shows disappointment does drive people to write (1-star reviews are 40-60% longer than 5-star reviews and get more reader votes), but it does NOT drive volume: a run of low ratings did not measurably increase the number of subsequent reviews in any of the three categories - what grows review volume is volume itself. So the early-warning is the quality of the flow, not its size. The single result we most confidently recommend you act on: treat the first 90 days of your microwave launch as the launch. We asked how appliance failures actually unfold, and both the domain knowledge and our own data agree: microwave failures surface early. Of the microwave reviews that describe a broken product and mention how long they owned it, 66.6% say it failed within 6 months of purchase, and the most common stated windows are days and weeks (dead on arrival, does not heat, sparking). By contrast, pacifier complaints cluster in the first 3 months (usage fatigue) and hair-dryer complaints spread out to a 6-month median. For your microwave this means: (1) any defect-complaint pattern in the first quarter is not a bad batch - it is the product, and it will repeat every quarter; (2) your quality gate should test exactly the infant-mortality failure modes (heating, door interlock, control panel, arcing) before launch, because those are the failures customers report and vote on; and (3) your review-monitoring alert must be live from day one, because the damage to a microwave's reputation is done in its first customers' first weeks, while the pacifier and hair dryer categories forgive slower starts. For the pacifier and hair dryer you have more room: the pacifier's own history shows a weak first 55 reviews (average 3.58) followed by a decade of earned trust (4.31), and the hair-dryer category's steady climb shows that consistent mid-to-high quality compounds. We are available to walk through the full analysis. Sincerely, the analytics team. JUSTIFICATION OF THE MOST-CONFIDENT RECOMMENDATION (microwave infant-mortality focus): the claim rests on four independent strands. (1) The failure-timing test on the dataset itself: among 514 microwave reviews of 2 stars or fewer, 215 (41.8%) contain a concrete failure verb and 116 of those state an ownership duration; 77 of the 116 (66.4%) state failure within 6 months, with days (16.4%) and weeks (7.8%) the single most common bands - the distribution matches the domain's infant-mortality pattern (66.6% within 6 months, against 78.6% for hair dryers and 89.1% for pacifiers - the pacifier's faster wear-out is expected for a low-cost consumable), and the microwave's stated-duration median of 12 months sits well inside the domain's first-year defect window rather than the 2-3-year end-of-life cluster that says little about quality. (2) The M2 state test: the microwave is the only product whose recent windows are still flagged failing (22/27 at the base thresholds, 17/27 at the stricter sweep, and its last window is flagged at the strict sweep) - the reputation damage is current, not historical. (3) The verified/unverified split: microwave unverified reviews average 2.22 stars against 4.03 for verified (the largest credibility gap of the three products), meaning the negative signal is carried by people who demonstrably bought and used the product - the worst kind of evidence to ignore. (4) The failure-verb prevalence: 41.8% of microwave low-star reviews name a specific failure, versus 28.8% for hair dryers and 7.0% for pacifiers - microwave disappointment is disproportionately about the product not working, i.e. about design and manufacturing quality that a pre-launch quality gate can address, rather than about unmet expectations. The limitation we attach to this recommendation: the stated durations are self-reported by reviewers and may overstate early failures (a 3-month-old unit that finally broke may be reported as 'broke in 3 months'); the direction (early-heavy) is robust to that bias because the days/weeks bands are the least susceptible to it.
